title: Set the human check for six teams
scenario:
Northfield Housing Trust rents homes to about 900 households. It has six teams. The director asked each team to write one line on how it wants to use AI, and asks you to check the plan before any tool goes live.

Use the exhibit. The trust, the teams and the plan are made up for this case. Facts about the tools and policies are from the vendors' docs, help pages and use policies, October 2026.
exhibit:
BRIEF (made up):
  Northfield Housing Trust, 70 staff, six teams.
  Goal: one page that says where AI helps and
  who checks it, before any tool goes live.

PLAN (draft AI use per team):
  HR:
    AI scores every job application and sends a
    "no" to the lowest half. Nobody reads them.
  LEGAL:
    AI summarises each new supplier contract
    with quotes and clause numbers. A lawyer
    reads the contract before anyone signs.
  FINANCE:
    AI writes the monthly cost note with its
    code tool on. "The tool did the maths, so
    we skip the spreadsheet check."
  TENANT SUPPORT:
    A website bot answers tenants day and night.
    It may promise repair dates and offer rent
    discounts by itself.
  TRAINING:
    New staff learn the rent rules with a tutor
    project. Its instructions say: "Always give
    the complete answer first."
  YOUTH CLUB (3 staff, 20 volunteers):
    Volunteers use their own free AI accounts
    and paste in the children's names and
    medical notes. Owner: "everyone".

questions.prompt: HR: what must change before the scoring tool is used?

options.text: Nothing, because a score is only a number and not a decision
options.explanation: Here the score sends a "no" with nobody in between. The Anthropic Usage Policy lists rejecting candidates as a high-risk use.

options.text: A qualified person reviews each score and can change it first
options.explanation: Right. Under the Anthropic Usage Policy, someone trained for the job must review each high-risk output, and be able to change it, before it is acted on.

options.text: The tool sends the "no" emails more slowly, over a full week
options.explanation: Slower emails are still decisions with no review. The timing is not the risk.

options.text: HR checks one rejected application in twenty, once a month
options.explanation: A sample after the fact skips most people. Review comes before each decision.

questions.prompt: FINANCE: is it safe to skip the spreadsheet check?

options.text: Yes, because a code tool runs code for every number it writes
options.explanation: The Claude docs say Claude answers simple arithmetic directly, without running code.

options.text: Yes, as long as the note says the code tool was switched on
options.explanation: A label does not make a number right. Each number still needs a check.

options.text: No, the note should be sent to the bank so it checks the maths
options.explanation: The check belongs inside the trust, before the note goes out, from the source file.

options.text: No, simple sums may skip the code tool, so a person re-checks each
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say simple arithmetic is answered without running code. So someone redoes each figure in a spreadsheet, from the original data.

questions.prompt: TENANT SUPPORT: what is the right change to the bot?

options.text: The bot gives dates and discounts only after the tenant asks twice
options.explanation: Asking twice does not give the bot the right to promise. The promise is still made with no one allowed to make it.

options.text: No promises from the bot: dates and discounts go to a person
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say a support agent should not make promises it is not authorized to make, and should hand cases that need a person to a person.

options.text: Keep the bot as it is, but only turn it on during office hours
options.explanation: The time of day does not change who may promise a repair date or a discount.

options.text: Let the bot promise dates, but add a small "AI" label to each
options.explanation: A label does not stop a tenant holding the trust to the promise.

questions.prompt: TRAINING: how should the tutor instructions change?

options.text: Keep them, since a complete answer saves new staff a lot of time
options.explanation: If the tool gives the answer first, the new staff copy it and learn little. The trainer sets the rules.

options.text: Remove them, so new staff can tell the tool how to help them
options.explanation: Without rules, a helpful tool still gives the answer when asked. The trainer writes the rules.

options.text: The tutor asks a question and gives a hint before any answer
options.explanation: Right. Project instructions apply to every chat in the project, so the trainer can make the tutor let staff try first.

options.text: Add a rule that every answer must be shorter than fifty words
options.explanation: A short answer is still an answer given before the learner thinks.

questions.prompt: YOUTH CLUB: what should the plan say?

options.text: One named owner, and a data rule: no children's details in AI
options.explanation: Right. A workflow needs one owner, and the team needs one clear data rule. The Claude Help Center warns about sharing health records in consumer plans.

options.text: Each volunteer chooses their own rule, since they know the children
options.explanation: Many private rules are the same as no rule. One clear rule is written for everyone.

options.text: Keep it all, but use only the first name of each child in the notes
options.explanation: First names with medical notes still point to real children in a small club.

options.text: Keep it all, as long as everyone deletes their chats every Friday
options.explanation: Deleting later does not undo sharing it now, and nobody owns the job.
